title: The Pombaline Reforms
titleline: The Pombaline Reforms - The History Web
para1: The Pombaline Reforms. Sebastiao Jose de Carvalho e Melo, the Marquis of Pombal, ruled Portugal for a generation (1750-1777) as the all-powerful minister of King Joseph I, and he ruled it as the age's most ruthless enlightened despot. When the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 destroyed the capital in minutes, Pombal's reply became the motto of his rule - bury the dead and feed the living - and he rebuilt Lisbon on a grid that still stands. Then he turned to the empire, and above all to Brazil.
para2: Pombal set out to make Portugal rich on its colony and free of England. He created monopoly companies for the trade of Para and Pernambuco, broke the power of the great nobles and the Inquisition's old families, expelled the Jesuits from the whole Portuguese world in 1759 - the destruction of the Guarani missions of Paraguay followed within the decade - and took the missions' lands and the education of the empire into the state's hands. In Brazil he abolished Indian slavery, transferred the capital from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro in 1763, and reorganized the Amazon as the new state of Grao-Para e Maranhao.
para3: The reforms shook Brazil's settled order. The expulsion of the Jesuits scattered the missions' hundreds of thousands of Indian charges; the new directors of the Indian villages tried to force assimilation; the monopoly companies and the new taxes fell heavily on the mining towns, feeding the discontent that erupted in the Inconfidencia Mineira of 1789. Yet Pombal's economic nationalism also built: new factories in Portugal, a modernized army, and in Brazil a tighter, richer, more centrally ruled colony whose trade boomed.
para4: Pombal fell with his king in 1777, and the reaction undid his companies and softened his Indian laws, but his Brazil endured: Rio the capital, the missions gone, the Amazon opened, the colony's wealth and self-confidence grown past the point of return. When the Portuguese court itself fled to Rio before Napoleon in 1808, it was Pombal's centralized Brazil that received a king - and, in 1822, became an empire of its own.

title: The Comunero Revolt of 1781
titleline: The Comunero Revolt of 1781 - The History Web
para1: The Comunero Revolt. In 1781, in the market towns of the Andean highlands of New Granada, in what is now Colombia, Spain's new taxes met a society at the end of its patience. The Bourbon reformers, determined to make the empire pay, had raised the sales tax, extended it to tobacco and aguardiente, and put the collection into harder hands. In the town of Socorro in March 1781 the crowds refused to pay, tore up the tax edicts, and the revolt spread town by town until a whole region was marching under captains elected in common - the comuneros.
para2: The rising found its leaders among the humbler gentry and the market-farmers: Jose Antonio Galan, the passionate organizer; Ambrosio Pisco; and the woman whose name the revolt kept, Manuela Beltran, the Socorro shopkeeper who tore the tax decree from the wall with her own hands. In May an army of perhaps twenty thousand comuneros - mestizo farmers, Indian villagers, poor whites - marched on Bogota itself, carrying banners of the Virgin and the king, demanding the taxes be repealed and Americans preferred to Spaniards in office.
para3: The capital, defenseless, yielded. At Zipaquira the royal commissioners signed the comuneros' demands - the Capitulations of Zipaquira - and the great host, believing it had won, went home. Then the viceroy disowned the capitulations, troops moved in, and the revolt was picked apart: Galan and the leaders were hanged and quartered in 1782, their houses razed, the salt tax kept. The far more terrible Indian rising of Tupac Amaru II in Peru, raging at the same months, had shown Madrid the price of conciliation - and of refusal.
para4: The comuneros were forgotten for a generation and then remembered as prophets. When New Granada rose against Spain in 1810, the patriots claimed the revolt of 1781 as their beginning, and later Colombians placed Manuela Beltran among the founders of the nation. The Comunero Revolt stands in the line that runs from the tax riots of the Bourbon empire to Bolivar: the first time Spanish Americans marched in tens of thousands against the crown - under the crown's own name, for rights they no longer believed it gave them.

title: Bolivar and the Liberation of the North
titleline: Bolivar and the Liberation of the North - The History Web
para1: Bolivar and the Liberation of the North. Simon Bolivar was a young Caracas aristocrat - rich, brilliant, educated in Spain, and sworn, he said, on the Monte Sacro in Rome in 1805 not to rest until America was free. When Venezuela rose in 1810 he was its colonel and its propagandist; when the First Republic fell and the royalists under the terrible llanero chief Boves drowned the Second in blood, Bolivar was driven into exile in Jamaica, where he wrote the Jamaica Letter of 1815, the prophecy of the American continent's destiny. He would be called, and called himself, the Liberator.
para2: His war was lost many times before it was won. Landing again in 1816, beaten again, driven to the Orinoco's edge, Bolivar rebuilt his cause in the plains: he raised the llanero horsemen who had destroyed his republics, welded them to the British Legion - five thousand veterans of Napoleon's wars who crossed the Atlantic to fight for him - and in 1819 attempted the impossible: he marched his army west through the flooded plains and over the frozen passes of the Andes, an ordeal that killed a third of his men, and fell upon the astonished royalists at Boyaca on 7 August 1819. New Granada was freed in a day.
para3: From Boyaca ran the chain of victories that freed the north: Carabobo in 1821, which secured Venezuela; Pichincha in 1822 under Sucre, which freed Quito; and the creation of Gran Colombia - Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador in one republic, with Bolivar as president. In 1824 his armies ended Spanish power in Peru itself at Junin and Ayacucho, and the liberated Upper Peru took his name: Bolivia.
para4: The union did not survive the peace. The vast republic strained apart under its jealousies; Bolivar's authoritarian constitution of 1828 and his lifelong presidency alienated his own generals; Venezuela and Ecuador seceded as he lay dying. In December 1830, on his way to exile, the Liberator died at Santa Marta, poor and embittered: he who has served a revolution, he wrote, ploughs the sea. Within a generation he was the hero of the whole hemisphere, and his dream of American unity has haunted its politics ever since.

title: San Martin and the Crossing of the Andes
titleline: San Martin and the Crossing of the Andes - The History Web
para1: San Martin and the Crossing of the Andes. Jose de San Martin was a Spanish officer - born in the River Plate, raised in the armies of Spain against Napoleon - who came home in 1812 to offer his sword to the revolution in Buenos Aires. He quickly saw what the porteno generals would not: that the independence of the south could not be won by attacking up the spine of Peru, where every patriot army had died. He proposed instead to cross the Andes, liberate Chile, take the sea, and come at Peru by water - the boldest plan of the wars of independence.
para2: He made it real at Mendoza. As governor of Cuyo, in the shadow of the mountains, San Martin spent two years building the Army of the Andes with a quartermaster's genius: five thousand men, made from freed slaves, frontier gauchos and Chilean exiles under Bernardo O'Higgins; forges casting cannon, women sewing uniforms by the thousand, mules and forage gathered pass by pass. In January 1817 the army marched - and in twenty days crossed the highest passes in the Americas, Uspallata and Los Patos, at altitudes that killed men and mules by the hundred, without losing a gun.
para3: The royalists of Chile were destroyed before they understood what had come over the mountains: Chacabuco, 12 February 1817, broke them; the patriot defeat at Cancha Rayada the next year was redeemed at Maipu, 5 April 1818, which secured Chile forever. Then the second half of the plan: the Chilean squadron under the cantankerous British genius Lord Cochrane swept the Spanish navy from the Pacific, and in 1820 San Martin's army landed in Peru. Lima fell in 1821, and San Martin proclaimed Peru's independence, ruling as Protector.
para4: The two liberators met at Guayaquil in July 1822 - alone, and no one recorded what passed. San Martin came out, resigned everything, and sailed for Europe, leaving the completion of the war to Bolivar: he never returned to power and died in Boulogne in 1850, in self-chosen obscurity. Argentina, Chile and Peru remember him as the greatest of their founders - the general who conquered three countries and refused to rule one.

title: Ayacucho and the End of Spanish Rule
titleline: Ayacucho and the End of Spanish Rule - The History Web
para1: Ayacucho. By 1824 the Spanish Empire in America had shrunk to its birthplace and its fortress: Peru, where the last viceroy still ruled from the highlands with the last royalist army. Bolivar, now Dictator of Peru, drove the war into the mountains. At Junin, on 6 August 1824, his cavalry broke the royalist horse in a charge fought with lance and saber alone - not a shot fired - and the initiative passed forever to the patriots.
para2: The decision came four months later on the plateau of Ayacucho, three thousand meters up in the Andes. On 9 December 1824 the royalist army under Viceroy Jose de la Serna, some nine thousand veterans with the best generals Spain had left, attacked the patriot army under Bolivar's lieutenant Antonio Jose de Sucre. The battle lasted an hour. Sucre's timing was perfect: the royalist advance overreached, the patriot counterstroke broke their center, and by afternoon the viceroy was a prisoner and his army was surrendering on terms.
para3: The Capitulation of Ayacucho was more than a surrender: La Serna gave up not only his army but the war - the whole of Peru, every garrison, and the royal cause in South America. The last holdout, the fortress of Callao, starved into 1826; Upper Peru, liberated by Sucre, became the republic of Bolivia in August 1825, taking its name from Bolivar and its first constitution from his pen.
para4: Ayacucho ended three hundred years of Spanish rule on the South American mainland. Spain kept only the islands of Cuba and Puerto Rico, and the marble of its American empire had become nine republics. Sucre, the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho at thirty-one, went on to be Bolivia's first president and to die by an assassin's bullet at thirty-five; the plain where he won is marked by a white obelisk, and Ayacucho remains, with Yorktown and Waterloo, one of the battles that closed an age.

title: Artigas and the Banda Oriental
titleline: Artigas and the Banda Oriental - The History Web
para1: Artigas and the Banda Oriental. On the east bank of the River Plate, in the grassland province the Spanish called the Banda Oriental - the modern Uruguay - the revolution of 1810 found its own liberator: Jose Gervasio Artigas, a former soldier of the frontier, a smugglers' countryman, and the idol of the gauchos. In May 1811 his ragged army of horsemen beat the Spanish at Las Piedras and besieged Montevideo, and the Banda Oriental rose for the revolution - but not, Artigas insisted, for Buenos Aires.
para2: That insistence made his tragedy. Artigas stood for a confederation of free provinces against the centralism of the porteno capital, and when Buenos Aires made peace with the royalists and ordered his people off the land to starve Montevideo, the Orientals answered with the Exodus of 1811: thousands of families abandoned their homes and marched into exile in Entre Rios rather than submit. For five years Artigas ruled the Banda Oriental from his leather tent at Purificacion, governing by handwritten regulation: his land decree of 1815, taking the land of enemies and giving the free poor - the gauchos, the blacks, the Indians - their share, was the most radical social measure of the American revolutions.
para3: His republic of gauchos was crushed between empires. The Portuguese of Brazil, fearing his example on their own frontier, invaded in 1816; Buenos Aires abandoned him; and in 1820, after four years of war, his last army was destroyed at Tacuarembo. Artigas rode alone into exile in Paraguay, where he lived thirty more years on a farm, refusing every offer to return, and died in 1850, two years after his country's independence.
para4: The nation he had dreamed rose without him: in 1825 the Thirty-Three Orientals landed to liberate the Banda from Brazil, and in 1828 Britain brokered the buffer state of Uruguay between Argentina and Brazil. But Uruguay's memory made Artigas its founder - the Protector of Free Peoples - and his gaucho army, his exodus and his land law stand at the root of the country's identity.

title: The Independence of Brazil and Pedro I
titleline: The Independence of Brazil and Pedro I - The History Web
para1: The Independence of Brazil. Brazil won its independence without a war of liberation, because its king was already there. In 1808 the Portuguese court, fleeing Napoleon, sailed to Rio de Janeiro under British escort - the first European monarchs to set foot in the Americas - and raised the colony to a kingdom in 1815. When King Joao VI was called home in 1821, he left his son Pedro as regent with famous advice: if Brazil must go, let it go with you, not with the rabble of the provinces.
para2: The Lisbon Cortes forced the issue. Determined to reduce Brazil to a colony again, it ordered the prince home and the provinces to obey Lisbon directly. Pedro refused: in January 1822 the Fico - I am staying - and through the year the Brazilians rallied to him. On 7 September 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga brook, he drew his sword and cried: Independence or death! The Grito do Ipiranga made Brazil independent; on 1 December he was crowned Emperor Pedro I. The provinces that resisted - Bahia, Para - were subdued by sea within two years by the hired British admiral Lord Cochrane, and Portugal itself recognized the empire in 1825.
para3: Pedro I's Brazil was an anomaly the Liberator envied: a constitutional monarchy that kept its unity, its territory and its peace while Spanish America shattered. But the emperor ruled by fiat and favorites, lost the Banda Oriental - Cisplatina - to war and independence in 1828, and quarreled with his Brazilian party over absolutism and Portugal, whose crown he briefly inherited and never gave up. In April 1831, after riots in Rio, he abdicated in favor of his five-year-old son Pedro II and sailed away to fight for his daughter's throne in Portugal, dying there in 1834.
para4: The regency decade that followed was turbulent, but the empire held; Pedro II, crowned early in 1840, reigned forty-nine years, abolished the slave trade, freed the womb in 1871, and presided over abolition in 1888 - the act that cost him the planters' support and, in 1889, the crown itself. Brazil passed from colony to kingdom to empire to republic with less blood than any nation of the Americas - the peculiar path of the Ipiranga.

title: The Peru-Bolivia Confederation and Its War
titleline: The Peru-Bolivia Confederation and Its War - The History Web
para1: The Peru-Bolivia Confederation. In 1836 the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho's successor in Bolivia, Andres de Santa Cruz, achieved what Bolivar had only dreamed: a union of Andean states. Santa Cruz - half-Quechua, born beside Lake Titicaca, president of Bolivia and the ablest soldier-statesman of the post-independence generation - had already reorganized Bolivia's finances, army and law. In 1835 he marched into a Peru torn by civil war, won the battles, and joined the two countries, and then the two Perus themselves, into a single Peru-Bolivian Confederation, with himself as Supreme Protector and Bolivian-directed power from Lima to La Paz.
para2: For three years the Confederation worked. Santa Cruz gave it order, free trade between its states, and the busiest diplomacy in the Pacific - and thereby made mortal enemies. The Chilean minister Diego Portales saw in the united Andes the end of Chile's commercial dominance of the South Pacific: Valparaiso could not compete with a protected Callao. Chile declared war in 1836; the Argentine strongman Juan Manuel de Rosas joined the coalition from the south; and Peruvian exiles - above all Agustin Gamarra, the defeated caudillo - joined the invaders.
para3: Santa Cruz beat the first Chilean expedition and took its surrender, magnanimously letting it go home. The second, better prepared, met him at Yungay in the Peruvian highlands on 20 January 1839, and there the Confederation died: the Protector's army was destroyed, Santa Cruz fled to exile, and Peru and Bolivia fell back into their separate, quarrelsome orbits. Portales, the war's author, had already been murdered by his own mutinous troops; Gamarra, restored in Peru, invaded Bolivia and was killed at Ingavi in 1841.
para4: Yungay closed the last serious attempt to unite the Andean republics, and it fixed the politics of the South Pacific: Chile's supremacy of the coast, confirmed forty years later in the War of the Pacific; Peru and Bolivia weakened toward their nineteenth-century ordeals. Bolivia still keeps the Confederation's memory as a lost great destiny - and Santa Cruz as the founder of its state.

title: The Federal War in Venezuela
titleline: The Federal War in Venezuela - The History Web
para1: The Federal War. Venezuela in the 1850s was a nation exhausted by its own heroes: three decades of caudillo rule since independence had brought debts, dictatorship and the rule of a conservative oligarchy of Caracas planters, while the plainsmen and peasants who had fought the war remained landless. In 1859 the Liberal Party rose under the slogan that gave the war its name and its program: Federation - a republic of states against the centralism of Caracas - and, as the fighting radicalized, lands for the landless.
para2: The war's driving force was Ezequiel Zamora, the chief of the plains, whose cavalry armies of llaneros made him for five years the terror of the oligarchy: he promised the land to those who worked it, and his horsemen carried federalism - and social revolution - through the interior until a stray bullet killed him at San Carlos in 1860. His brother Gabriel and then the guerrilla commander Juan Crisostomo Falcon carried on the war, which ground through sieges, massacres and devastation for four years and cost Venezuela, by the usual count, over a hundred thousand dead.
para3: It ended in 1863 with the Treaty of Coche: the oligarchy yielded, Falcon entered Caracas as president, and the constitution of 1864 made Venezuela a federation of twenty sovereign states - the United States of Venezuela. The Liberals had won; and within a decade the victorious generals, Antonio Guzman Blanco above all, had rebuilt the centralized dictatorship in Liberal dress, while the land stayed where it had been.
para4: The Federal War was the bloodiest of Venezuela's nineteenth-century wars and the defining trauma of its century: it destroyed the old conservative order, enthroned federalism in name, and taught the country's political class that the llanero masses could be raised - but never quite rewarded. Its memory fed the long line of strongmen that ran from Guzman Blanco to Cipriano Castro and Juan Vicente Gomez, who ruled Venezuela into the 1930s.

title: Uruguay's Guerra Grande
titleline: Uruguay's Guerra Grande - The History Web
para1: The Guerra Grande. The little buffer republic of Uruguay was born divided: between Montevideo, the port, liberal and commercial, and the interior of the cattle ranches; between the followers of the first president, Fructuoso Rivera - the Colorados - and those of his successor, Manuel Oribe - the Blancos. In 1839 Rivera, backed by the Argentine dictator Rosas's enemies and by French gold, declared war on Oribe, and the two Uruguayans and their foreign paymasters turned the country into a battlefield for thirteen years: the Great War.
para2: Its siege became the sensation of the age. Oribe, supplied by Rosas from across the river, besieged Montevideo for nine years - the Troy of America, its defenders called it - while the city held out behind its walls, provisioned from the sea, defended by a legion of Italian volunteers under a young Garibaldi and by French and British squadrons that twice intervened against Rosas outright. The countryside belonged to the Blancos' gaucho cavalry; the city and the world belonged to the Colorados.
para3: The war drew in the whole Plata: it was at bottom the long duel between Buenos Aires under Rosas and everyone who resisted him, and it ended only when Brazil, fearing Rosas's hegemony, joined the anti-Rosas alliance, and the Entre Rios strongman Urquiza turned on his master. In 1851 the allies crossed into Argentina; at Caseros, on 3 February 1852, Urquiza destroyed Rosas's army, and the siege of Montevideo was lifted. Oribe went into exile; the Colorados kept the capital.
para4: The Guerra Grande cost Uruguay a generation and much of its people, and fixed its politics: the division into Colorado city and Blanco interior ran through every later conflict, down to the civil war of 1904, and the two parties still bear the names born in the war. And it taught the powers of the Plata that Uruguay's fate would always be decided as much in Buenos Aires, Rio and London as in Montevideo.

title: The Chincha Islands War
titleline: The Chincha Islands War - The History Web
para1: The Chincha Islands War. In 1864 Spain, flexing old muscles in the Pacific during the American Civil War, sent a scientific expedition with a powerful squadron to South America's west coast - and in April its admiral abruptly seized the Chincha Islands of Peru, the guano islands whose bird-droppings, shipped to Europe as fertilizer, were the richest export in the Pacific. The pretext was an affront to Spanish immigrants; the purpose, every South American believed, was empire again. The seizure raised the continent.
para2: Peru, its government wavering, found itself at war; Chile closed its ports to the Spanish squadron and was bombarded into war too; Ecuador and Bolivia joined the alliance of the four Pacific republics. On 7 February 1866 the allies beat a Spanish division at Abtao, and on 31 March Admiral Mendez Nunez, frustrated by Chile's refusal to submit, bombarded the open port of Valparaiso, burning its undefended waterfront - an act that shocked the world's conscience and emptied Spain's diplomatic credit.
para3: The war's last act made Peru's pantheon. On 2 May 1866 - a date Peru keeps as a national day - the Spanish squadron bombarded the defenses of Callao, and the Peruvian guns, served by artillerymen and minister of war alike, answered so fiercely that the squadron, its admiral wounded, withdrew from the South Pacific for good. The ironclad age had announced itself at Callao's roads: it was the first battle between armored ships and forts in the Americas.
para4: The war settled nothing legally - formal peace treaties dragged into the 1870s - but everything politically: Spain never again threatened its lost colonies by force, and the Pacific republics, briefly united, had tasted an American alliance against Europe. Within a decade, though, Peru and Chile would be at war with each other, and the guano that had been worth a squadron would be nearly gone.

title: The Guano Era in Peru
titleline: The Guano Era in Peru - The History Web
para1: The Guano Era. Off the desert coast of Peru, on the rainless Chincha Islands and the points of the shore, the seabirds of the Humboldt Current had been leaving their droppings for ten thousand years, until the guano lay in deposits a hundred feet deep. In the 1840s European agriculture discovered that nothing on earth fertilized like it, and for four decades Peru possessed the nearest thing to a money tree any nation has had: by the 1850s guano was three-quarters of the state's revenue, and the government of Peru lived by selling mountains of bird-dung to the farmers of Europe.
para2: The bonanza transformed Peru. President Ramon Castilla, the strongman of the guano's first age, used it to free the slaves in 1854 - indemnifying their owners - and to end the Indian head-tax; railways crept from Lima toward the mines, a telegraph followed, the capital rebuilt itself in Parisian taste, and a swollen state payroll and foreign loans consumed what the birds provided. The digging itself was done by Chinese contract laborers, brought in their tens of thousands on coolie ships to work the islands in conditions remembered as a new slavery.
para3: It could not last. The deposits were worked out by the 1870s just as Peruvian finances drowned in debt and synthetic fertilizers undercut the remainder. Worse, the guano had distracted Peru from the neighboring desert that would decide its fate: the nitrate fields of Atacama, where Peruvian and Chilean capital contested the next fertilizer fortune - the contest that ended in the War of the Pacific in 1879 and the loss of Peru's nitrate provinces.
para4: The Guano Era is Peru's great lesson in the wealth of nations: a generation of prosperity that built railways and freed slaves, that financed a war and a standing army - and that vanished with the birds' deposits, leaving the debts behind. Peruvians call the whole mid-century simply la era del guano, and its rise and fall still frame the country's memory of easy riches and hard reckonings.

title: The Amazon Rubber Boom
titleline: The Amazon Rubber Boom - The History Web
para1: The Amazon Rubber Boom. Deep in the Amazon forest, the Hevea tree wept a white sap that the peoples of the forest had used for centuries - and which the industrial world, from the 1880s, suddenly could not live without: rubber for the tires of the bicycle and then the automobile. The only place on earth it grew wild was the Amazon, and for thirty years the basin of the greatest river became the scene of one of the most feverish booms in history. Manaus, a river-port of a few thousand, became by 1900 a city of electric trams, electric light and an opera house in Italian marble, where the rubber barons lit cigars with banknotes.
para2: Behind the opera house was the rubber estate, and behind the estate, the seringal. The system was debt-slavery in the green hell: collectors - tappers - recruited from the drought-starved northeast of Brazil and from the indigenous peoples, carried hundreds of miles upriver, bound by debts to the trading houses, and set to walk the estradas through the forest from tree to tree, bleeding the latex into cups. Mortality was enormous; and where labor would not come, it was hunted: the enslavement and extermination of the forest peoples, above all in the Putumayo, reached a savagery that Roger Casement's report of 1912 exposed to a horrified world.
para3: The boom made and unmade nations' maps: Bolivia's Acre territory, rich in rubber, was taken over by Brazilian tappers who proclaimed their own republic and, after three wars of skirmish, were bought out by Bolivia's sale of Acre to Brazil in 1903. Iquitos in Peru, Leticia, and a hundred river towns lived on the latex price; a third of the Amazon's people, by some counts, were gathered into the seringais.
para4: It ended as suddenly as it rose. In 1876 the Englishman Henry Wickham had carried seventy thousand Hevea seeds from the Tapajos to Kew Gardens, and by 1913 the plantations of British Malaya - orderly, efficient, safe - had broken the wild rubber price forever. Manaus's opera house closed its doors; the barons vanished; the forest towns went back to the river. The boom left the Amazon's boundaries drawn, its peoples decimated, and its cautionary tale: the jungle's riches, the Brazilians say, are caboclo's gold - gone in a hand's turn.

title: Ecuador's Liberal Revolution of 1895
titleline: Ecuador's Liberal Revolution of 1895 - The History Web
para1: Ecuador's Liberal Revolution of 1895. For a generation Ecuador had been the most clerical state in the Americas: Gabriel Garcia Moreno, the devout strongman assassinated on the cathedral square in 1875, had consecrated the republic to the Sacred Heart, made the Church the partner of the state, and left his conservative successors ruling a theocracy in miniature. In 1895, after a stolen election, the coast rose. Guayaquil - liberal, commercial, anticlerical, and long resentful of the mountain capital - proclaimed the revolution, and General Eloy Alfaro, the veteran radical in exile, came home to lead it.
para2: The revolution was swift and total. Alfaro's army entered Quito in September 1895, the conservatives were driven from power, and for the next sixteen years - the two terms of the Old Fighter himself and those of his Liberal successors - Ecuador was remade: church and state separated, civil marriage and divorce introduced, education secularized, religious orders curbed, the vote and the press widened. Alfaro's other work was steel: the Guayaquil-Quito railway, the audacious line that climbs from the coast over the Andes by the Devil's Nose switchbacks, completed in 1908, bound the two Ecuadors - coast and sierra - into one country for the first time.
para3: The Liberals governed by the sword as much as by statute, and Alfaro's own end showed the savagery beneath the politics: overthrown in 1911 and returned from exile to fight again, he was defeated, shipped to Quito as a prisoner, and in January 1912 a mob dragged Eloy Alfaro and his fellow generals from the prison and burned their bodies in the public park - the night Quito's elite avenged itself on the old revolutionary.
para4: The revolution of 1895 endured past its maker. Liberal rule lasted until 1925, and its settlement - the secular state, the coast-sierra axis, Guayaquil's weight in the nation - defined modern Ecuador. Alfaro, ashes and all, is the country's liberal founding father: the railway he built still crosses the Devil's Nose, and his statue stands where his pyre was lit.

title: Chile's Civil War of 1891
titleline: Chile's Civil War of 1891 - The History Web
para1: Chile's Civil War of 1891. Chile after the War of the Pacific was the dominant power of the South Pacific, rich on nitrate - and locked in a constitutional duel between its president and its congress. Jose Manuel Balmaceda, elected in 1886, was a president of grand designs: railways, schools, public works on a scale the nitrate boom could finance, and a determination to keep the nitrate wealth in Chilean hands. To a congress of nitrate interests and parliamentary principle, he was a would-be dictator; when it refused him a budget, he ruled without one, and in January 1891 congress proclaimed him deposed.
para2: The country split by its armed forces: the navy declared for congress, the army for the president. The congressional squadron seized the nitrate ports of the north, raised an army of its own, and in eight months of war - the battles of Concon, where the congressionalists stormed ashore, and Placilla, in August 1891 - destroyed the presidential army. Perhaps ten thousand died, among them the flower of two generations of Chilean officers, many killed by their own cadets and classmates.
para3: Balmaceda would not survive his defeat. Sheltering in the Argentine legation as the victors entered Santiago, he wrote his testament - I am not defeated, my cause will triumph - and shot himself on 19 September 1891, the day after his legal term ended. His death made him what his life could not: the martyr of the presidential ideal, and the idol of every later Chilean strongman.
para4: The victors built the Parliamentary Republic that ruled Chile for a generation: a government by party caucus and cabinet crisis, nicknamed by its enemies the rule of the senores. It brought prosperity, corruption and drift until the new century's discontents swept it away, but 1891 settled the central question of the Chilean state - no king in Santiago - at a price in blood that Chileans never forgot, in the only civil war Chile has fought as a republic.
